generatedProse.concept-context: The School of Sport gives you material of very different shapes, and the three families fit different shapes. A structure with linked parts, such as the anatomy of a joint or the stages of tissue healing, suits a visual map that shows how the parts connect. A set of clinical terms, special-test names or definitions suits flashcards or reading aloud. An assessment or treatment protocol, which is a sequence of steps, suits a kinaesthetic walk-through. Choosing well means looking at the material first.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport therapy students revise the same module, which has three very different topics: the anatomy of the knee, a list of special-test names, and the steps of a rehabilitation assessment.

Tom likes flashcards, so he makes flashcards for all three. The test names suit cards well. But the anatomy of the knee becomes a pile of cards in no order, and the links between the structures are lost. The assessment, which only makes sense as a sequence, does not fit cards at all. The technique was fine; using the same one for everything was not.

Amara looks at each topic first. The special-test names become flashcards. The anatomy of the knee becomes a map that lays out the structures and shows how they connect. The rehabilitation assessment becomes a physical walk-through, stepping through each stage in order. Each technique was chosen to fit what the topic is.

Both students revised all three topics. Only Amara matched the technique to the material rather than forcing one method onto everything.
generatedProse.summary: Active techniques fall into three families: visual, auditory and kinaesthetic. In sport therapy, a linked structure suits a visual map, a set of terms suits flashcards or reading aloud, and an assessment protocol suits a kinaesthetic walk-through. None is better than the others; the skill is matching the technique to the material. You can now describe the families, place a technique in its family, and choose techniques that fit what you are revising.

check.body: In the worked example, why did Amara use a map for the knee anatomy and flashcards for the special-test names?

items.text: She matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than using one method for everything.
She preferred variety and wanted her revision to feel less boring.
She had run out of flashcards and had to improvise.
Maps are always better than flashcards in sport therapy.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara chose each technique to fit the kind of material, which is selecting to fit.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the reason that is about matching the method to the material.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara matched each technique to the kind of material, rather than forcing one method onto everything. It was not about variety, chance or one technique being best.
